checklist.title: New home checklist
checklist.subtitle: Details that make adaptation easier.
items: Protective screens on windows and balconies.
Litter box in a quiet spot.
Food bowls away from the water.
A bed or safe resting space.
Scratchers and enrichment toys.
Consistent feeding routine.
Vaccination plan and trusted vet.
Daily time for interaction and affection.

stories.title: Situations that guide the choice
stories.subtitle: Educational examples; these are not user testimonials.

items.text: A quiet routine and smaller home may call for a compatible cat and an enriched environment.
A shy cat may need a safe space, a predictable routine, and gradual contact during the first weeks.
Living with other animals requires controlled introductions, supervision, and a way to keep them apart.

faq.title: Questions for a real adoption
faq.subtitle: Use these answers as a starting point and confirm everything with the responsible organization.

items.q: Do I need experience with cats?
items.a: Not necessarily. Check whether the organization offers guidance and whether you can meet the animal’s needs.

items.q: Can I adopt if I rent?
items.a: Confirm the property rules, install suitable protection, and check whether the space fits the cat’s profile.

items.q: How long does a real adoption take?
items.a: Timing varies by organization, screening, and animal. This project does not conduct or estimate real adoption processes.

items.q: How can I confirm the cat’s health?
items.a: Ask the real responsible party for veterinary records and confirmation of vaccines, neutering, deworming, and special needs.

hero.title: What responsible adoption involves
hero.subtitle: Assess your routine, costs, safety, and long-term commitments before contacting a real organization.

items.title: Your routine
items.text: Consider the available time, budget, and changes that daily care will require.

items.title: The cat's needs
items.text: Plan for a protected environment, veterinary care, and resources suited to the animal's profile.

items.title: Responsible organization
items.text: Verify who is responsible for the cat, which information is documented, and how post-adoption support works.

list.title: Before adopting
items: Confirm that the home allows animals and can receive suitable safety protection.
Plan recurring expenses and an emergency fund for veterinary care.
Assess the time available for interaction, cleaning, and enrichment.
Consider children, other animals, and foreseeable changes to the routine.
Verify the organization's identity and the source of information about the cat.
Understand the adoption agreement and the support offered after adoption.

facts.title: What to ask about the cat
facts.subtitle: The responsible organization should confirm the real animal's history and needs.

items.title: Health and history
items.text: Ask for veterinary records, feeding information, and details of any ongoing care.

items.title: Observed behavior
items.text: Ask which behaviors were observed and in which environments, without treating the profile as a guarantee.

items.title: Adaptation
items.text: Confirm how to prepare for arrival, introduce other animals, and request guidance if difficulties arise.

hero.title: Prepare for a responsible adoption
hero.subtitle: Review questions, care needs, and steps to confirm with the organization responsible for the animal.

requirements.title: What to confirm with the organization
requirements.subtitle: Each organization defines its own criteria. Ask why each requirement exists and how your data will be used.
items: Which documents are requested and why.
Which safety conditions the home must meet.
Whether follow-up visits will occur and how they will be arranged.
Which vaccines and veterinary care are required.
How much daily time the cat will need for interaction and enrichment.
Which commitments are included in the responsible adoption agreement.

support.title: Support after adoption
support.text: Ask who can provide guidance during adaptation, through which channels, and for how long.

tips.title: First days at home
tips.subtitle: Tips to help your new friend feel safe and welcomed.

items.title: Restricted space at first
items.text: Keep the cat in a quiet room for a few days, with food, water, and a litter box, so they get used to the new smells.

items.title: Hiding spots are important
items.text: Cats feel safer when they have somewhere to hide. Cardboard boxes or 'cave' type beds are excellent for the first weeks.

items.title: Patience and space
items.text: Let the cat come to you. Forcing affection or picking them up in the first days can cause stress. Sit on the floor and wait for their curiosity.

hero.title: Privacy Policy
hero.subtitle: Understand which data stays in the browser and which external services are accessed.

content.title: Data in the demonstration stage
content.text: Catlovers does not submit or store data entered in the form. Language and theme stay in the browser’s local storage, and a cat fact may stay in the session. Unsplash images, the catfact.ninja API, and GitHub Pages hosting may receive technical request data under their own policies. Before any real collection, this policy must define purpose, retention, rights, and a responsible contact.

article.title: How to introduce a new cat to other pets
article.p1: The arrival of a new feline in the house is always a moment of joy, but it requires a lot of patience and planning, especially if you already have other cats or dogs.
article.p2: Never put the animals face to face on the first day. Reserve a room in the house just for the newcomer. They will need their own litter box, water bowls, food, and places to hide.
article.p3: Before seeing each other, they should smell each other. Rub a clean towel on the new cat and place it near the food bowls of the resident animals, and vice versa. This way they will associate the other's smell with something positive (food).
article.p4: After a few days of peace, allow them to see each other through a crack in the door or a baby gate. If there are hisses or growls, close the door and try again the next day.
article.quote: The biggest mistake owners make is rushing the introduction. Feline time is very different from ours.
article.p5: When there are no longer aggressive reactions through the crack in the door, let them be in the same environment, always with supervision. Offer treats so they associate each other's presence with good times.
